title: Fall Garden Cleanup: What I Cut, What I Leave, What I Plant
creator: Jo Whitfield Gardens
description:
First frost is coming! My October jobs: clearing blighted tomatoes, leaving seed heads for the birds, mulching the beds and planting spring bulbs.

Bulbs from Rootstock Seeds, 15% off with code GARDENJO: https://rootstockseeds.com

The pollinator mix: crocus, allium, tulip 'Queen of Night'.

sentences.t: It's the middle of October, the first frost is coming this weekend, and the garden looks like a crime scene.
So today I'm doing my big fall cleanup, and I'll show you what I cut back, what I leave, and what I plant now for spring.
First up, the tomatoes.
These are done, they've got blight on the lower leaves, and the last few fruit are never going to ripen out here.
I pick everything that's showing even a little color and ripen it on the windowsill.
The green ones become green tomato chutney, which my husband pretends to like.
The plants themselves come out, roots and all.
And because of the blight, these do not go on the compost heap.
They go in the green bin for the council to take, because a home compost heap doesn't get hot enough to kill it.
Next, the perennials.
A lot of people cut everything down to the ground in the fall, and I used to do that too.
Now I leave most of the seed heads standing, the echinacea, the sedum, the grasses.
Birds eat the seeds all winter, and insects overwinter in the hollow stems.
Plus, honestly, frost on a seed head in January is one of the prettiest things in the garden.
What I do cut back is anything that's gone mushy or diseased, like this hosta, which is basically soup now.
Then the beds get a blanket.
I spread about two inches of leaf mold and compost over everything that's bare.
The worms pull it down over the winter, and by spring the soil is dark and crumbly.
And now the fun part, which is planting for spring.
This year all my bulbs came from Rootstock Seeds.
They're a small grower, and everything ships in paper bags with the planting depth printed right on the label, which, for someone like me who loses every plant tag, is a lifesaver.
I got their spring pollinator mix, it's crocus, alliums, and these gorgeous dark purple tulips called Queen of Night.
The bulbs are huge, look at this one, it's bigger than a golf ball, and that's what gives you big flowers.
They also guarantee them, so if something doesn't come up in spring, they'll replace it.
If you want to grab some before the ground freezes, use code GARDENJO for fifteen percent off at rootstockseeds.com.
Okay, planting.
The rule of thumb is three times as deep as the bulb is tall.
So for these tulips, that's about six inches down, pointy end up.
I plant them in clumps of seven or nine, never in neat little rows, because rows look like a car park.
Alliums go at the back of the border, because they get tall.
Crocus I just toss onto the lawn and plant wherever they land, so it looks natural.
Then a bit of chicken wire over the top, because the squirrels in this garden have no shame.
Last job, the tools.
Clean them, oil them, and hang them up, because a rusty pair of secateurs in March is a sad way to start the season.
That's my fall cleanup.
Let me know what you're planting for spring in the comments, and I'll see you next time.
